notes.meaning: Jesus calls His twelve followers close and gives them power and authority in His name. He equips them to drive out evil spirits and heal every kind of disease and sickness. These miracles served as signs to prove their message came from God and showed that the gospel brings spiritual healing to sick souls.

Jesus gives these twelve disciples the title of apostles, which means messengers sent out on a mission. Simon is listed first, given the name Peter, meaning a rock, alongside his brother Andrew. Next are James and John, the two sons of Zebedee.

differ.view: Peter was first in order on the list, but this gave him no command or special rule over the rest of the apostles.
Peter is named first because he was called early and helped keep the list in order, not because he held authority over the other apostles.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Listing Peter as first points to his unique leadership and authority over the apostles and the universal church.

notes.meaning: The list of messengers continues with Philip and Bartholomew, who is likely the man named Nathanael elsewhere. Thomas is paired with Matthew, who humbly reminds readers that he had been a despised tax collector before Christ saved him. James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus, also called Judas the brother of James, are named next.

Simon the Zealot had belonged to a Jewish group known for fierce political and religious zeal before following Jesus. Judas Iscariot is placed last, bearing the shameful note that he was the one who would betray the Lord. Jesus knew what Judas was from the beginning, but chose him to show that false believers can exist even within the church.

Jesus sends the Twelve out with strict boundaries about where they may go. For this short first trip, they are forbidden from going into non-Jewish Gentile lands or entering Samaritan cities. God planned for the message of salvation to be offered to the Jewish people first before spreading across the wider world.

Instead of traveling to other nations, the disciples are told to seek out the lost sheep of Israel. The Jewish people were wandering in sin and error because their religious leaders had failed to shepherd them properly. Jesus felt great pity for them and sent His messengers to guide them back to God.

As the disciples travel from town to town, their main task is to proclaim a royal announcement like town heralds. Their core message is that the kingdom of heaven is close at hand. They called on people to turn away from their sins and prepare for the rule of the Messiah.

Jesus tells the apostles to heal the sick, restore people with severe skin diseases, raise the dead, and drive out demons. Since they received this supernatural power freely without paying a penny, they must never charge money or use it for personal profit. Their free acts of mercy showed that God's salvation is a free gift of grace.

The apostles are forbidden to pack gold, silver, or copper coins in their money belts. They were not to delay their start by raising funds, nor should they seek to get rich from their journey. Jesus wanted them to travel light and learn to trust God completely for their daily needs.

They were not to take a traveler's food bag, extra clothing, spare sandals, or a defense stick for the road. The people who heard their message were expected to provide food and shelter for them. A faithful worker earns the right to his daily meals, so ministers may rightly expect their basic physical support from their work.

Upon entering any town, the disciples were to look for an upright person of good character who feared God and would welcome the truth. Once they found lodging, they were to stay in that same home until moving on to the next village. Staying put kept them from wandering about like idle beggars or seeking out wealthier hosts.

When the apostles walked up to any home, they were commanded to greet the household with warmth and courtesy. In Jewish culture, this meant offering the customary blessing wishing peace to the family. True religion teaches believers to be civil, polite, and kind to everyone they meet.

If the family proved receptive and welcomed the messengers, the blessing of peace would rest upon them and bring God's favor. If the household rejected them, that offered peace would return to the disciples themselves. God's servants will never lose their own blessing even when their goodwill is turned down by others.

If a house or an entire town shut its doors and refused to listen, the disciples were to shake the dust off their feet as they walked away. Jewish travelers did this when leaving foreign pagan lands to avoid carrying unclean dirt into the holy land. Doing this against fellow Jews showed that their rejection of the gospel placed them on the same level as unbelieving heathens.

Jesus solemnly warned that it would be more bearable on judgment day for the ancient cities of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that rejecting town. Those old cities were destroyed for terrible wickedness, yet they had far less light than people who heard the apostles in person. Rejecting the open offer of Christ's salvation brings greater guilt and heavier condemnation.

Jesus warned that He was sending His followers out like helpless sheep into the middle of vicious wolves. Because real danger was everywhere, they needed to be shrewd like snakes, using caution to avoid unnecessary traps. At the same time, they were to stay innocent like doves, refusing to use deceit or harm others to save their own skin.

The disciples were told to be on their guard because people would turn hostile against them. Religious leaders would arrest them, drag them before local courts, and whip them in the very synagogues used for worship. Jesus foretold these hardships so His followers would not be caught by surprise or lose their faith when attacked.

Because of their loyalty to Jesus, the disciples would also be brought before top provincial rulers and powerful kings. These harsh trials were not accidents, but divine opportunities to witness to high officials and Gentile nations. Standing on trial allowed poor fishermen to preach the gospel where it had never been heard before.

When handed over to judges and rulers, the disciples were instructed not to worry or panic about what to say. They did not need to craft clever legal speeches beforehand, because God would provide the right words at that very moment. Christians can face sudden trials with peace, trusting the Lord to supply wisdom when the crisis arrives.

Jesus comforted them by explaining that they would not be defending the faith alone. The Holy Spirit of their heavenly Father would speak through them with wisdom and power. God ensures that His servants are never left defenseless when they stand up to speak for Him.

Persecution for the gospel would shatter even the closest family ties. Brothers would betray brothers to execution, fathers would hand over their children, and children would rise up to have their parents put to death. The world's deep hatred of Jesus is so fierce that it can overcome even the natural love of relatives.
